items.originalTitle: Inside the battle to lead the RNC after its midterm wipeout
items.author: Aaron Pellish, Erin Doherty and Andrew Howard
items.title: Inside the battle to lead the RNC after its midterm wipeout
items.summary: The chair of the Republican National Committee is scrambling to avoid becoming the party’s midterms scapegoat. With President Donald Trump’s backing, Joe Gruters would normally be a lock to retain his position as RNC chair. But after this month’s brutal midterm losses, he is now trying to fend off an upstart and surprisingly strong challenge from co-chair KC Crosbie ahead of the January leadership election. As both candidates jockey behind the scenes for support, deep divisions have emerged between members over who bears responsibility for the wipeout earlier this month and what comes next. Party leaders have been reluctant to publicly point fingers at Trump and his unpopular agenda. Instead, conversations with more than two dozen RNC members and operatives familiar with the committee’s dynamics reveal that some are channeling their frustration toward Gruters. Even as his supporters argue he’s being unfairly blamed for a difficult political environment, Gruters could still become the fall guy. For some of Gruters’ critics, the decision is simple: Someone must pay for the once-unthinkable losses. “It is time for new leadership. That's nothing against Joe at all,” said Kentucky GOP Chair Robert Benvenuti, who plans to vote for Crosbie. “But different times require different leadership, different types of leaders.” An undecided RNC member added: “There's an awful lot of anger.” That member, granted anonymity to speak candidly about private conversations, described members questioning whether to “rubber stamp the guy that rightly or wrongly is seen as the architect of this mess.” The debate within the RNC — whether to break with the Trump-backed candidate or stick with the status quo — mirrors the broader reckoning underway in the GOP over how closely to align with the president moving forward. Many Republicans have resigned themselves to Trump’s continued dominance over the next two years, but some RNC members have already begun to agitate for change in other ways, including by calling for an autopsy of the midterms and for congressional leadership elections to be delayed. Several RNC members said Gruters helped the committee raise millions this cycle, arguing that alone is a key part of his job and he handled it well. Others were frustrated that the RNC didn’t engage or spend money in their states earlier. And some members criticized Gruters for allowing the RNC to become overly enmeshed in the White House’s political operation. “The party raised a lot of money, and we spent it. I don't think that there's a whole lot of that that can be laid at [Gruters’] feet,” said West Virginia GOP chair Josh Holstein, who said he has not yet committed either way in the leadership race. “At the same time, I know there's a lot of members of the committee that feel we need to go a different direction, and that the RNC needs to be a little more autonomous in its decision making.” The RNC and Crosbie declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Gruters campaign said in a statement that RNC members “are rallying behind Chairman Gruters because they know he will never stop fighting for Republicans.” “Chairman Joe Gruters has 25 years of experience at every level of the Republican Party, shattering fundraising records, building the largest election integrity operation in party history, and advancing President Trump’s agenda,” the campaign said. The outcome of the leadership race, which will be determined by a secret ballot, will test just how far RNC members are willing to go to change course — even if it means defying Trump. And the stakes are enormous, with the RNC playing a key role in the presidential race, including running the GOP primary debates, hosting the party’s 2028 convention and supporting the eventual nominee. Complicating the calculation is Trump’s own involvement: The president has been a vocal supporter of Gruters and has privately suggested that if Crosbie wins the leadership battle, he wouldn’t assist the RNC with fundraising ahead of 2028, according to two people familiar with the threat who were granted anonymity to speak about private details. The threat was first reported by Axios . It’s an apparent acknowledgement that even Trump knows it’s a real contest — and that his chosen candidate may become a scapegoat. Vice President JD Vance, who also serves as the RNC’s finance chair and is considering a presidential bid, has privately offered to assist Gruters’ reelection campaign, according to a person with direct knowledge of the outreach granted anonymity to speak about private details. Gruters has not yet taken Vance up on his offer, the person said. Vance’s office did not respond to a request for comment. “There is an element that is concerned about this underlying President Trump support, and if we don’t vote for his guy, we’re undermining the president and further giving him more bad news, black eyes, and there’s some sensitivities to that,” said a second RNC member who is undecided about the leadership election and granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive political dynamics. “But you also have some that are more protective of the brand and the party than they are to the person, especially given the results of this last election cycle,” the person said. Trump allies have been checking in with RNC members to gauge where they stand in the leadership race, said the RNC member, who received such a call. It’s not yet clear where the membership stands. Both Gruters’ and Crosbie’s camps are keeping their whip counts closely guarded in part to avoid a repeat of the 2022 RNC chair election, when allies seeking to oust former chair Ronna McDaniel aggressively badgered party members in hopes of elevating Harmeet Dhillon. “I think it's going to be a close race,” said Holstein, the West Virginia GOP chair. Behind the scenes, both candidates have been courting RNC members. Gruters has called people to solicit their support and leaned on both Trump’s endorsement and the consequences of Trump pulling out of future RNC fundraising. Rhode Island GOP Chair Allyn Meyers said Gruters sent him and the state’s other RNC members the president’s Truth Social post giving him his “complete and total endorsement.” “You don’t fire your best salesman because he’s got a bad quarter,” said Illinois GOP chair Bob Grogan, who plans to support Gruters. Crosbie, for her part, has sent a 10-12 page detailed survey to RNC members asking specific questions about the timing of when resources were deployed to their state this cycle and about staffing, among other areas, according to three people familiar with the survey. In conversations with undecided party members, Crosbie has pledged greater transparency into the party’s finances, one of the people said. She is also making her case to members who are frustrated by the party’s perhaps too close coordination with Trump world and want to have greater say in the RNC’s strategy. The RNC has historically operated as a political arm of the president whenever a Republican is in the White House. “You want the coordination, you want the closeness and the efficiency of it,” said Washington GOP chair Jim Walsh, who did not share who he’d be supporting in January. However, he added: “You want those two to be two different heads, two different brains, two different hearts, and you want a little tension there because you riff off each other on how you should proceed on a campaign or on a cycle strategy.” A national GOP strategist who supports Gruters pushed back on the calls for a more independent RNC. “This is not Model UN. It’s about winning elections,” said the person, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. Whether they plan to vote for Gruters, Republican Party chairs from red and blue states alike told POLITICO the midterm results raise the need for a serious reckoning over the role the RNC should play in future cycles — and how it appeals to a broader swath of the electorate. “Regardless of who the chair is, I think there has to be changes in the way the committee operates,” said Ben Proto, Connecticut’s GOP chair, who did not share who he would be supporting in January. “The committee has to look beyond those, you know, in 2024, it was the seven states. In 2026, it was the highly targeted areas. I think we have to broaden our approach to the electorate. We have to look at 50 states.” “We took a pretty good beating two weeks ago or so,” said Benvenuti, of Kentucky. “And in my view, that should cause deep reflection about how the organization should be run, how messaging should be done, how the organization should function internally.” Lauren Fedor contributed reporting.

items.summary: What makes people support a carbon price? To find out, 108 researchers, led by a research team at the University of Innsbruck, Austria, tested 55 different ideas at the same time, from information campaigns to reflection tasks. On average, there was a small but statistically significant positive effect. Individually, the effect was detectable for only 11 of the 55 ideas. One of the strongest effects came from writing a letter to a fictional person of a future generation. The results were recently published in the journal Nature Human Behaviour.

items.originalTitle: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
items.author: Phil Hoad
items.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
items.summary: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood , now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024).

items.originalTitle: ‘I had to reject a lot of shame’: Michaela Yearwood-Dan on queerness, Catholicism and her extravagant artist dinner parties
items.author: Florence Hallett
items.title: ‘I had to reject a lot of shame’: Michaela Yearwood-Dan on queerness, Catholicism and her extravagant artist dinner parties
items.summary: The artist adorns her luscious paintings with diaristic notes and confessions. Ahead of an exuberant new show she discusses their unique creation method – and the hunt for her missing cat The artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evoke the ritual space of a church.

items.originalTitle: Toddlers are not just little people. Their culture deserves respect | Arwa Mahdawi
items.author: Arwa Mahdawi
items.title: Toddlers are not just little people. Their culture deserves respect | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary: Small children do not appreciate it when you join in with their singing or throw away their pee-covered leaves. And only a brute would suggest one of them might be tired Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs. As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I immediately went down an online rabbit hole and discovered various other people have made similar jokes . It’s a common issue.

items.originalTitle: An Ode to the Endeavour Space Shuttle
items.author: Marsha Ivins
items.title: An Ode to the Endeavour Space Shuttle
items.summary: Space Shuttle Endeavour in its launch position at the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center on Nov. 13, 2026. —Myung J. Chun—Los Angeles Times/Getty Images I’m standing on the floor of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center of the California Science Center under the tail of the new exhibit of the Space Shuttle Endeavour and remembering how I felt looking up at that same shuttle on the launch pad at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. There is no one word to describe that feeling: wonder, awe, amazement, immense pride that we could build and fly such a machine. How was this my job, I think to myself. I’d spent a large part of my NASA career as an astronaut supporting shuttle missions at the Kennedy Space Center; testing the vehicles about to fly; packing equipment bags for flight; sitting in a shuttle on the launch pad before the tank was fueled; ensuring switches were in the right positions; even strapping crews in before launch. As an astronaut, I had the opportunity to be strapped in myself on five shuttle missions, two on Columbia, and three on Atlantis . And for the decade prior to being selected into the astronaut office in 1984, I worked as an engineer at the Johnson Space Center on the development of this very spacecraft. Suffice it to say space was my jam and Shuttle my focus. Before a launch, the support structure is rolled away, and the shuttle stands alone, illuminated in bright lights. Everyone, save the handful of closeout and flight crew, is moved to 5 miles away. The vehicle sits fueled and alive, releasing small clouds of condensation from the tanks of cryogenic propellant, the epitome of potential energy. There is a quiet, intense anticipatory charge to the atmosphere. Standing now at the base of a stacked space shuttle in a museum, I am still moved by this extraordinary embodiment of technical audacity. The story of the Space Shuttle often seems like an abbreviated footnote in NASA’s history, homage still paid to the Apollo program. Interest is now focused on the anticipated return of Americans to the moon with the Artemis Program. Authorized in the 1970’s after Nixon canceled the Apollo program, the Space Shuttle was the world’s first reusable spacecraft, with all major components except the external fuel tank designed to be recovered and reused. It was billed at the time as taking spaceflight into the everyday realm of air travel, allowing access to orbit for all commercial, scientific, and military payloads. The contract for four flight vehicles and one atmospheric test vehicle went to the company Rockwell (now Boeing) in 1972. In 1977, that test vehicle, Enterprise, made its first of five free-flying approach and landing tests from the back of a 747, to demonstrate that a 200-ton glider with the aerodynamic performance of a cinder block could, in fact, be safely, successfully, and repeatedly landed on a conventional runway. In 1981, the first of the orbital shuttles, Columbia, made its maiden flight, flying 28 missions until its tragic accident during reentry in 2003. Challenger , the second shuttle to be built, made its first flight in 1983 and was lost on ascent during its 10th flight in 1986. The third vehicle, Discovery, launched in 1984, completed a record 39 missions before its final flight in 2011. The fourth vehicle, Atlantis, launched in 1985, completed 33 missions, ending the Shuttle program with its final mission in 2011. And then there was Endeavour. Born as a replacement for Challenger in 1987 and built largely from structural spare parts delivered as part of the original contract, Endeavour made her maiden flight in 1992, flying 25 missions, retiring in 2011. At the end of the shuttle program, after 135 flights, the decision was made to send the remaining orbital shuttles to museums and display them in the three flight configurations. Discovery rests on the ground in landing configuration at the Udvar-Hazy Center of the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum. Atlantis hangs in the Kennedy Space Center Visitor’s Complex in glorious flight configuration. And finally, Endeavour in launch configuration is now housed in a dedicated building, itself a structural work of art. The spacecraft rests on the last external tank built and two flight solid rocket boosters. And though it will live now as a static displayed part of space history, Endeavor is, nonetheless, still breathtaking. Seen from one angle as you enter the room, it sits in full pre-launch glory. Seen from another angle, one payload bay door open, the insulation material and the structure underneath can be seen. Ride the glass elevator to the very top, and you can see the view looking down on the entire stack, a view only those people working on the launch pad can typically see. It was at the base of the display, standing a hand's distance from the tip of the tail, looking up at this impossible realization of 35 years of Shuttle history, that I realized the lump in my throat had not dissolved for my entire tour. Where once she stood on the launch pad eager to fly, Endeavour stands now forever static, potential energy forever spent. But she remains an inspiration for ingenuity and determination; a tribute to those audacious ideas made reality, and to the technical firsts in human spaceflight. She still demands respect and humbling appreciation for the thousands of people in the NASA and contractor workforce whose minds and hands got those of us who flew to the pointy end. She serves as a living memorial to the hearts and souls of lives lived and lost. And now Endeavour, along with Discovery and Atlantis, lives on as a reminder of a capability in human spaceflight we no longer have.

items.originalTitle: How the War Turned Sudan Into a Country Without a Newspaper
items.author: Isma’il Kushkush
items.title: How the War Turned Sudan Into a Country Without a Newspaper
items.summary: Ahmed Aman, a Sudanese man, who spoke about being imprisoned and tortured in Rapid Support Forces' prisons before fleeing El-Fasher, sits at a makeshift shelter in the town of Tawila Sudan's Darfur region on March 2, 2026. —AFP-Getty Images A war of narratives is being waged within the war in Sudan. The warring parties—the official Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force—are fighting an information war through traditional and social media. Misinformation, disinformation, hate speech, and propaganda are routinely deployed, and Sudanese journalists have become targets. Thirty-four journalists have been killed in Sudan in the past three and a half years of war. Sixteen of them are believed to have been targeted for their journalistic work. Hundreds of journalists h ave been displaced with their families and lost their jobs; dozens have been threatened , assaulted, and detained. Most of the Sudanese newspaper offices, television studios and radio stations have been looted, damaged, or destroyed. For the first time in over a century, Sudan has gone without a single newspaper being printed in more than three years. Yet Sudanese journalists have worked hard to inform the world of the costs of the war in their country: more than 400,000 people are estimated to have been killed; 12 million are believed to have been displaced; widespread destruction, looting, hunger, and human rights abuses have ravaged the African nation of 53 million people. The war has effectively divided Sudan into two zones of control : the SAF holding around 60% of the territory concentrating in eastern and central Sudan , and the RSF controlling about 40% of the country concentrating in Darfur and adjoining areas in southern and western Sudan. Both the SAF and the RSF maintain a tight control over what can be reported from the areas they control. The New York Times reported that SAF used banned chemical weapons in the war, and a UN fact-finding report accused the RSF of s exual violence and slavery and described its violence in El- Fasher as bearing the “defining characteristics of genocide." Seeking credible information from the ground has turned Sudanese journalists into targets. In July, the Sudanese Journalists Syndicate (SJS) and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) submitted a report to the U.N. Human Rights Council on the regression of press freedom and the intimidation of journalists during the war in Sudan. “The war came with a knockout punch to the press,” recalled Abdelmonium Abouedries, a veteran journalist and chairman of the SJS. “Truth became the war’s first victim.” A heroic reporter in El-Fasher On Oct. 10, 2023, Halima Idris Salim, a correspondent for Sudan Bukra, an independent non-profit media platform, was reporting on the dire conditions of a hospital in the city of Omdurman, northwest of the capital Khartoum. An RSF vehicle ran over her on a street and killed her. The Sudanese army wasn't innocent either. In December 2024, the SAF arrested Yahya Hamad Fadlallah and his son at their home in Khartoum. An editor, columnist, and novelist, Fadlallah was celebrated for his novel Zugendi’s Marriage in Sudan. According to the SJS and Darfur Bar Association , he was falsely accused of collaborating with the RSF, tortured, and denied treatment for diabetes in detention. After being released on Jan. 10, 2025, Fadlallah was admitted to a hospital, but died there three days later. Apart from the killings, Sudanese journalists have faced threats and criminal charges for their work. In May, Rishan Oshi, a journalist with AlBalad TV, a private television network, was sentenced to a year in prison and fined $16,553 for defamation by a court in Port Sudan. The charges against her were filed after she posted an article about government corruption on her popular Facebook page. The costs of reporting on active hostilities can be dangerously high. In April 2025, the Sudanese military took back control of Khartoum, but the war intensified in the Darfur region. The RSF had besieged the city of El Fashir in Darfur to consolidate their control over the region. Mouammar Ibrahim , a freelance reporter for Al Jazeera Mubashir, reported on the long siege and the terrible human conditions in the city. The RSF shelled and attacked the city with drones, enforced starvation and blocked aid. Some people survived on animal feed. A famine stalked El-Fashir and its displaced people, living in camps nearby. Days before the fall of El-Fashir in Oct. 2025, Ibrahim tried to leave the city with thousands of others. The RSF fighters identified, abducted, and detained him. The paramilitary force proceeded to kill, detain, and disappear thousands as it captured the city. In a social media video, the RSF authorities claimed that they were investigating Ibrahim's "biased" reporting and that he would face a trial. "The journalist is a victim of arbitrary detention,” said Martin Roux of Reporters Without Borders, “held in conditions that pose a grave threat to his life.” Honoring bravehearts Yet despite these grave difficulties, Sudanese journalists have carried on reporting on the war and other political and social stories that continue to affect lives in their country and earned well-deserved recognition for their bravery. Salma Abdel Aziz, an independent journalist, reported on the imprisonment and murder of violence young girls and women by their families in Darfur for possessing mobile phones. Her reporting won her the Intergovernmental Authority on Development Media Award. Zeinab Mohammed Salih, an independent journalist, reported on the eruption of war from Khartoum for The Guardian, The Financial Times, and the BBC. She was the first journalist to report and verify the 2023 Geneina massacres in Darfur, where thousands were killed. She also reported from El-Fasher before its fall. Salih was awarded the 2026 ICJF Knight International Journalism Award. In the chaotic opening weeks of the war, AlMidgad Hassan, a pharmacology graduate with some media training, started reporting for Alhadath, an Arabic news network, which is part of the Saudi Al Arabiya network. His first report was from inside a bombed apartment in Khartoum using a smart phone held by a friend. He continued to report for Alhadath for three years, often seen in a helmet and flak jacket around war-torn Khartoum. For his work, he was awarded the 2026 Press Freedom Unlimited Newcomer of the Year Award . In 2026, he moved on to work for Aljazeera English. Four stories of Sudan won at the 2026 One World Media Awards in London, which honors reporting on the Global South. Mohammed Amin, a Sudanese journalist won One World Media ’s Journalist of the Year Award for his reporting on how villagers in central Sudan defended themselves against the RSF. But Amin was denied a visa to the United Kingdom to receive his prize. “The Sudanese are not a heavy burden on this world but insisting to be equal partners in humanity,” he said in a video message. Sudanese media groups were also recognized for their work during the war. Ayin Network, whose editors relocated to Kenya won the One World Media Press Freedom Award, as its reporters continued to report from Sudan publishing their work without bylines for their safety. The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate , a journalist union, was awarded the 2026 UNESCO/Guillermo Cano World Press Freedom Prize Award for its work in highlighting the struggles of Sudanese journalists, documenting attacks on the press, and defending Sudanese journalists. “I had nothing but tears,” Abouedries, the chairman of the SJS, told me, describing it as a moment of “pride and joy.” Awards alone cannot end Sudan’s war or the suffering of its people, but the attention, solidarity and commitment to truth they encourage can help. Silvia Chocarro, a senior strategic advisor to the International Press Institute (IPI) who lived in Sudan, told me, “When Sudanese journalists receive international recognition, there is a very powerful message: we see you, your work matters, and you are not alone.”

items.title: New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010
items.summary: The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025. The main drivers are sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law.
